name: Hydroquinone
lead: Hydroquinone (benzene-1,4-diol) is a phenolic compound applied to the skin to lighten dark patches. People use it to even out skin tone where melasma, sun spots (solar lentigines) or post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, such as marks left after acne, have left areas darker than the surrounding skin, either alone or in combination creams with a retinoid and a corticosteroid.[1][2][24] Outside dermatology it is best known as a photographic developing agent and a polymerization inhibitor; the name was coined by Friedrich Wohler in 1843.[1]

Several reviews describe it as the long-standing reference treatment for hyperpigmentation: a 2022 systematic review calls topical hydroquinone the gold standard in melasma, and a 2020 evidence-based review found a triple combination cream (hydroquinone, tretinoin and a corticosteroid) and hydroquinone alone to be the most effective melasma treatments among those examined.[3][4] Newer agents such as tranexamic acid, thiamidol and azelaic acid have been compared against it in randomized trials with mixed relative results, and a 2026 Delphi consensus of dermatologists from 11 countries addresses where it sits in current management.[2][5][6][19]

Its regulation is contested and differs by country. Wikipedia reports that the US FDA withdrew over-the-counter hydroquinone in 2020 while prescription products remain available, and that European Union rules from 1976 restrict it to prescription use; reviews and other encyclopedia entries describe a ban on cosmetic use in the EU, Japan and Australia.[1][2][23] Documented adverse effects include contact dermatitis and, with prolonged use, exogenous ochronosis, and the compound has been the subject of safety reviews over absorption and carcinogenicity questions.[1][2][25]

paras: People use hydroquinone to lighten dark patches from melasma, sun-induced lentigines and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, and it appears in photoaging regimens alongside botanicals and peptides in cosmeceutical reviews.[2][7][8] It is typically applied to the affected spots rather than the whole face, an approach Wikipedia's skin-whitening article also describes for isolated marks such as moles.[23] Dermatology sources pair it with strict daily sun protection, because ultraviolet and visible light can stimulate pigment and bring patches back.[24]

It is also found in combination products. The triple combination of hydroquinone, tretinoin and a corticosteroid is described in Wikipedia's melasma article as working better than dual combinations or hydroquinone alone, and a 1975 trial by Kligman combined 5 percent hydroquinone, 0.1 percent tretinoin and 0.1 percent dexamethasone for melasma and related pigmentation.[1][4][24]

Outside medicine, hydroquinone is a main component of black-and-white photographic developers, a polymerization inhibitor and an antioxidant intermediate.[1] A beetle species, the bombardier beetle, uses hydroquinone and hydrogen peroxide in its defensive spray, a topic that appears in unrelated T Nation evolution threads.[1][9][10]

Other agents used for the same patches include azelaic acid, kojic acid, retinoids, cysteamine, glycolic acid peels, lasers and oral tranexamic acid, according to Wikipedia's melasma and hydroquinone entries; Wikipedia's hydroquinone article also reports that 4-butylresorcinol has been shown to be more effective and is considered safe enough for over-the-counter sale.[1][24] The same melasma entry notes that intense pulsed light can darken melasma.[24]

Hydroquinone is used in dermatology as a depigmenting agent. Melasma, a chronic condition marked by brown to gray-brown facial patches, is the main target; it is more common in women and in people with Fitzpatrick skin types III and above, and it is described as relapsing, with sun exposure a common trigger.[24] Hydroquinone is available over the counter at 2 percent or by prescription at 4 percent in the United States, according to Wikipedia's melasma entry, though the OTC route was changed by the 2020 FDA reform described below.[24][1]

Hydroquinone has been reported to improve melasma. A narrative review cites a 2020 report of 96 percent improvement with 3 percent hydroquinone twice daily plus sunscreen versus 81 percent with hydroquinone alone, and a 30-person study in which 2 percent hydroquinone-cyclodextrin lightened solar lentigines over two months; the review itself notes its evidence base is small studies, and that effects typically appear after about 5 to 7 weeks with courses of at least three months in melasma.[2]

Comparator trials give mixed relative results. In the review's summary, 4 percent hydroquinone acted faster than kojic acid, while 3 percent tranexamic acid produced a greater reduction in MASI and melanin index than 4 percent hydroquinone in one trial, and 0.2 percent thiamidol outperformed 2 percent hydroquinone in another.[2] Other randomized trials have compared thiamidol with 4 percent hydroquinone in 50 women,[5] tranexamic acid cream with hydroquinone in a split-face design,[6] and tranexamic acid/niacinamide creams with hydroquinone.[11] A systematic review states that the superiority of microneedling and peels to hydroquinone remains to be established and that recurrence rates remain high in all treatment groups.[3]

Wikipedia's melasma entry describes the condition as chronic and relapsing, with small amounts of sun exposure able to bring pigment back after it fades; this matches the review observation that recurrence rates are high across treatment groups.[3][24]

Human trials include comparisons with thiamidol (n=50),[5] with 3 percent tranexamic acid in a double-blind split-face trial,[6] with niosomal and conventional tranexamic acid/niacinamide creams,[11] with kojic acid and azelaic acid in melasma,[2][12] and a registered trial against miconazole (n=60),[13] a 4 percent cream phase 3 study (n=17),[14] hexyresorcinol versus hydroquinone for photoaging (n=32),[15] and several comparisons against other formulas and oils.[16][17]

Systematic and consensus reviews include a review of 113 controlled studies with 6,897 participants (2020),[4] a 2022 systematic review,[3] a 2024 update on new and existing melasma treatments,[18] and a 2026 Pigmentary Disorders Society Delphi consensus with 38 dermatologists from 11 countries.[19]

Reviews list allergic or irritant contact dermatitis, hypopigmentation and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation as short-term effects. Exogenous ochronosis, a blue-black or gray-brown pigmentation of sun-exposed skin, is described as the most frequent effect of chronic use and largely permanent, although dermabrasion and laser treatment have helped in some cases.[2][20] Less common reports include trimethylaminuria, nail hyperpigmentation, reduced skin elasticity, impaired wound healing and peripheral neuropathy.[2]

On systemic safety, the review states that hydroquinone is absorbed through skin, that rodent studies show DNA damage and a few human cases of squamous cell carcinoma are on record, and that there is insufficient evidence that topical use causes cancer in humans; it advises pregnant or breastfeeding individuals to limit exposure.[2] Wikipedia reports that the FDA concluded in its regulatory review that carcinogenic potential could not be excluded, citing rodent tumour findings and absorption in humans.[1]

Wikipedia's ochronosis entry describes exogenous ochronosis as an acquired, avoidable condition caused by long-term topical phenol derivatives, most notably hydroquinone. It says risk rises with duration, most cases follow years of use and cases have been reported at concentrations as low as 2 percent; lesions progress from erythema and mild pigmentation to caviar-like lesions and then papulonodular lesions, usually on sun-exposed skin. Management centers on stopping the product, some studies report benefit from Q-switched alexandrite laser, and the condition can be mistaken for melasma, so that further hydroquinone is prescribed.[25]

Wikipedia's skin-whitening article adds that hydroquinone is absorbed quickly through the skin, that long-term use has been linked to kidney toxicity and benzene-related leukemia in some reports, and that it can interfere with capillary blood glucose meters, giving falsely high readings; it also states hydroquinone has not been officially classified as a carcinogen.[23] The US National Toxicology Program found 'some evidence' of carcinogenic and genotoxic effects according to Wikipedia's hydroquinone article, which lists rodent findings including thyroid follicular hyperplasia, leukemia and liver and kidney adenomas.[1]

Hydroquinone is oxidized by tyrosinase in preference to tyrosine, lowering melanin formation. The review also describes disruption of the melanocyte cytoskeleton and melanosome transport and inhibition of DNA and RNA synthesis, and suggests this disruption may contribute more than tyrosinase inhibition; it also scavenges free radicals.[2]

Wikipedia's melasma entry summarizes hydroquinone as inhibiting tyrosinase, the enzyme needed to make melanin, while its ochronosis entry describes phenol deposition in connective tissue altering collagen and elastin as the mechanism of that adverse effect.[24][25]

Hydroquinone is a white granular solid with two hydroxyl groups para to each other on a benzene ring. It is made industrially from 1,4-diisopropylbenzene via a cumene-like process or by hydroxylating phenol, and it can be reversibly oxidised to benzoquinone.[1]

Its skin-lightening effect was first reported by Oettel in 1936; in 1953 Lerner described a sunscreen formulation sold in the southern United States in which lightening was noticed as an unplanned side effect, and Spencer trialed it for hyperpigmentation in 1961.[1] In 1975 Kligman trialed the hydroquinone, tretinoin and dexamethasone combination for melasma and related disorders, which became the template for later triple creams.[1][4]

Wikipedia reports that the FDA classified it as generally recognized as safe and effective in 1982, revoked that approval and proposed an over-the-counter ban in 2006, and banned it in 2020 as part of an over-the-counter drug review reform.[1] Wikipedia's ochronosis entry places the first hydroquinone-induced ochronosis cases in 1975, with a phenol-related case reported in 1912.[25]

Wikipedia states hydroquinone is prescription-only in EU member states under a 1976 cosmetics directive, whereas a 2023 review states its use is banned in the EU, Japan and Australia, and Wikipedia's skin-whitening and ochronosis entries describe the EU as banning it from cosmetics in 2000.[1][2][23][25] In the US, over-the-counter products are not FDA-approved after the 2020 reform and the compound remains available as a prescription pharmaceutical.[1] In 2023 it was the 274th most prescribed medication in the US, with over 800,000 prescriptions.[1]

Wikipedia's skin-whitening article reports that lightening creams have commonly combined hydroquinone, mercury and potent corticosteroids such as clobetasol, and that products found in places such as Pakistan have been reported to contain toxic levels of hydroquinone and mercury.[23] It describes South Africa as regulating lightening products from the 1970s, banning those with mercury or high hydroquinone levels, and says that in countries where such products are restricted they continue to be sold, sometimes without declared ingredients.[23] It reports Indian skin-lightening cream sales of about 258 tons in 2012 and about US$300 million in 2013.[23]

These market and health concerns are distinct from clinical use of supervised prescription hydroquinone for melasma, though regulators and reviewers discuss them together when considering restrictions.[2][23]

T Nation users mention it in small numbers: one poster used a hydroquinone product for about four months to even skin tone, and another used it with tretinoin and pulsed dye laser on steroid-related acne scars.[21][22] It is discussed as a tone-evening ingredient alongside retinoids and sunscreen rather than as a central topic.

timeline.event: Name hydroquinone coined by Friedrich Wohler.[1]
A phenol-related ochronosis case is reported, per Wikipedia.[25]
Lerner describes lightening as a side effect of a sunscreen sold in the southern United States.[1]
Kligman trials hydroquinone, tretinoin and dexamethasone for melasma; hydroquinone-induced ochronosis cases are identified.[1][25]
FDA classifies hydroquinone as generally recognized as safe and effective, per Wikipedia.[1]
The EU bans hydroquinone from cosmetics, per Wikipedia's skin-whitening entry.[23]
FDA revokes previous approval and proposes over-the-counter ban.[1]
FDA bans over-the-counter hydroquinone in drug review reform, per Wikipedia; a systematic review of 113 controlled studies is also published.[1][4]
A Pigmentary Disorders Society Delphi consensus on melasma management with 38 dermatologists from 11 countries is published.[19]

lore.intro: Hydroquinone appears only occasionally in forum material, as a pigment-evening ingredient in skin-care and acne-scar threads; most claims about it come from dermatology reviews and consumer-safety debates.[21][22]

claims.claim: Hydroquinone is the strongest dark-spot treatment
claims.believers: Posters mention using it to even skin tone and for scars.[21][22]
claims.experts: Systematic reviews describe it as the gold standard and as among the most effective melasma treatments, though newer agents have outperformed it in some trials and recurrence remains high.[3][4][2]

claims.believers: Consumer-safety groups such as the Campaign for Safe Cosmetics have raised concerns, per Wikipedia.[1]
claims.experts: The FDA could not rule out carcinogenicity from rodent data and human absorption, while a review says evidence is insufficient to show topical use causes cancer in humans.[1][2]

claims.claim: Long-term or high-strength use can darken the skin permanently
claims.experts: Reviews list exogenous ochronosis as the most frequent effect of chronic use and largely permanent; Wikipedia says cases are mostly after years of use and are hard to treat.[2][20][25]

claims.claim: Hydroquinone alone is enough; adding sunscreen is optional
claims.believers: Some users treat the cream as the whole routine.
claims.experts: Dermatology sources say UV and visible light stimulate pigment and recommend broad-spectrum protection; a 2020 report cited in a review found 96 percent improvement with hydroquinone plus sunscreen versus 81 percent with hydroquinone alone.[2][24]

claims.claim: Newer agents like tranexamic acid or thiamidol have replaced hydroquinone
claims.believers: Proponents of newer actives point to head-to-head trials where they performed as well or better.
claims.experts: Trials report mixed results: 3 percent tranexamic acid and 0.2 percent thiamidol outperformed hydroquinone in some, while others found comparable effect; reviews still describe hydroquinone as a reference treatment.[2][5][6]

claims.claim: Imported or unlabeled lightening creams with hydroquinone are equivalent to prescription products
claims.believers: Sellers and users of such creams describe them as the same ingredient at lower cost.
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports creams in some markets contained hydroquinone together with mercury or clobetasol and undeclared ingredients, with documented health problems.[23]

chain: Pigmented areas lighten over weeks to months
angle.text: Hydroquinone is applied to specific dark areas, such as melasma patches, sun spots or acne marks, to lighten them toward the surrounding skin. Users and dermatology reviews describe visible change after roughly five to seven weeks, with courses of at least three months in melasma, usually alongside daily sunscreen.[2][24]
